meta.title: Twelve seats
meta.kicker: the crew an AI product needs before it survives a paying customer
meta.lede: An AI product needs about twelve seats filled before it can work properly with a paying customer. Most do not need a full-time person. One person can hold several of them for a while — that is what keeps a crew small, and it is why some problems surface late. Two of the seats cannot be replaced by engineering.
meta.howto: For each seat: what it owns, how you know the work is done, what happens while it is empty, and who has to work next to it. Where a seat says covered, I have done that work and the evidence is linked. Where it says open, you need a separate person — and those two are the ones I would hire first.
meta.scope: This is about crews of three to fifteen people building a product with an LLM in it. In a company of four hundred these are departments and many of the answers change.
meta.portraits: Roles are named the way the market names them; the emoji is a marker, not a mascot.

roles.owns: Turning an unfamiliar domain into requirements you can build against: understanding how it works from the client's point of view before anyone writes code.
roles.measured: How much gets rebuilt after the first release meets a real user.
roles.empty: Engineers try to infer the domain from a single feature request. The product ships quickly into a demo, turns out to be wrong in structure, and the team cannot say why for months.
roles.grades: senior → lead. There is no junior version: the job is knowing what not to build.

evidence.text: Clinic front desk: a patient dialogue is a state machine that speaks natural language. Separating the booking from the conversation with the patient is what made quality testable.
Sixteen years reading other people's ledgers, contracts and asset registers — forensic analysis where the conclusion had to survive cross-examination in an arbitration court.
Two more domains I studied from outside: elections in a volunteer community and a data-analysis curriculum in edtech.

roles.limit: I can understand a domain if a practitioner explains how it works. I cannot replace that practitioner: I have never treated a patient, and I know the difference between a model of a clinic and the clinic.

complement.seat: The design partner — a real practitioner inside the domain
complement.why: I can only understand what I am shown. So you need someone inside the domain who explains regularly how the work really goes and corrects my assumptions. One available practitioner is worth more than three advisors with impressive titles.
complement.when: Before the first line of code. Without that person you have a hypothesis, not a product.

roles.owns: The product itself: dialogue orchestration, retrieval, agentic pipelines, integrations and the other technical parts that hold it up.
roles.measured: Whether the product works for someone who was not involved in building it.
roles.empty: Nothing exists. Everything else on this page is a plan.
roles.grades: mid → senior. A mid can build the main scenario; the senior work starts at the seams.

evidence.text: An LLM platform for clinics: in five months I took it from an empty repository to production with a live client. It has deterministic dialogue orchestration, retrieval over clinic knowledge, a booking state machine and operator handoff.
Lua in production on roughly 1.4 million Wikipedia pages — code maintained by strangers, where a bad edge case is visible to everyone.

roles.limit: One product in production with live client traffic. I have not run a system under load heavy enough to make scale itself the main engineering problem, and I say so before anyone asks.

complement.why: I build the system and its seams. The interface is separate work, and a good system can lose to a worse one that is easier to use.
complement.when: The first hire after the engineer, in any product with a user interface.

roles.owns: Checking the claim 'it works', and the evidence that survives someone looking for the error.
roles.measured: Whether a quality regression is caught by the rig before it is caught by a customer.
roles.empty: Quality gets judged by eye. Every release becomes a bet, and the team gradually avoids changing the system because nobody can tell whether it got better.
roles.grades: senior. What matters here is memory of what has already broken.

evidence.text: A behavioural regression rig where simulated patients talk to the bot and a calibrated LLM judge scores every dialogue — 5300+ automated tests, judge running on a local GPU at zero cloud cost.
Before that: sixteen years where a conclusion had to hold up in an adversarial process, not a slide review. Evals are the same discipline with a newer object.
Detecting manipulation in 49,286 votes across nine years of community elections — and building the criteria that separate an anomaly from ordinary behaviour.

roles.limit: A judge scores against criteria. I can build the rig and calibrate it, but I cannot decide what counts as a good result in medicine or law.

complement.seat: The domain specialist who owns the scoring criteria
complement.why: The standard is not mine to invent. In a clinic that is a clinician; in finance, an auditor. Without them the rig measures self-consistency and calls it quality.
complement.when: As soon as the rig exists. Two hours of their attention a week — not a full seat, but those two hours are the whole value of the rig.

roles.owns: Where the tokens go, what one conversation costs, and what the system is doing right now.
roles.measured: Cost per unit of result, and how long it takes to find the cause of a failure.
roles.empty: The bill arrives before the understanding. Nobody can answer 'is this feature profitable' or 'why was last Tuesday bad'.
roles.grades: mid → senior. Setting up metrics is mid work; deciding what is worth measuring is not.

evidence.text: End-to-end cost observability for every LLM call, and the unit cost of a dialogue as a number rather than an intuition.
Moving the judge to a local GPU — a cost decision made because the cost was visible. That is the whole point of this seat.

roles.limit: Observability is not availability. I set up metrics, diagnose failures and cut cost. A 24/7 on-call rotation against an uptime SLA is a separate seat.

complement.why: Knowing what broke and being contractually responsible for it not breaking are different jobs with different sleep schedules.
complement.when: At the first customer with an SLA in the contract.

roles.owns: Whether the thing can make money, and the point at which that stops being a guess.
roles.measured: Whether the model matches the real invoice three months later.
roles.empty: The price is set out of thin air. A round is raised on a story the numbers contradict, and the problem surfaces in due diligence.
roles.grades: founder-level or fractional. Rarely a full-time hire before series A.

evidence.text: Unit economics of an LLM product modelled for investor negotiations — built on the per-call cost data rather than on assumptions.
Sixteen years of econometric models, audits and distressed-asset workouts, where the numbers were read by someone paid to find the hole in them.

roles.limit: I model what a customer has to pay for the economics to work. What a customer is actually willing to pay is a question about the market, and that needs a sales person.

complement.why: A model gives you a floor for the price; only a sales conversation gives you the ceiling. The two seats should argue every week, and they should not stay in the same head for long.
complement.when: Immediately. This is the pair that decides whether the company exists.

roles.owns: Raw material — collecting and cleaning the data everything else is built on.
roles.measured: How much of the pipeline another person can run on their own.
roles.empty: Analysis runs on one person's laptop and dies with their laptop.
roles.grades: mid. Senior only when volume or freshness becomes the constraint.

evidence.text: Sixteen years of getting data out of other people's ledgers, registries and contract archives — the extraction and cleaning half of forensic work.
49,286 votes across nine years of Wikipedia arbitration elections — collected, entity-resolved and published as an open dataset on Kaggle.
Vacancy and skills corpora assembled for analysis; teaching the data-wrangling half of an analytics curriculum for four years.

roles.limit: I build datasets and pipelines another person can run without my help, and I publish them. A platform that runs unattended on a schedule and needs someone on call when it breaks is a different job: operations, not assembly.

complement.why: Assembling data once and maintaining a pipeline with an SLA are different jobs. My approach stops working when the data has to stay current.
complement.when: When a pipeline must run unattended on a schedule and someone notices within an hour if it does not.

roles.owns: Which model to pick, when a prompt or retrieval is enough and when fine-tuning is needed, and what the benchmark actually measures.
roles.measured: Decisions that still work after the next model release instead of needing a rewrite.
roles.empty: The stack gets chosen by whatever was visible that month, and chosen again the next.
roles.grades: mid → senior, narrow. The senior part is knowing when no research is needed at all.

evidence.text: Selecting and calibrating the judge model against human-agreed scores; designing retrieval over clinic knowledge with its failure cases written down.

roles.limit: I select models, compare them and integrate them into the product. I do not train models, and I do not treat reading papers as a substitute for having trained one.

complement.why: Needed the moment the honest answer is 'train something', not 'choose and wire something'.
complement.when: Most AI products never reach that line. Work out whether you need a research seat at all before hiring for it: a year of a researcher on a product that needed integration work is expensive.

roles.owns: What happens to other people's data, and what the product is allowed to promise.
roles.measured: The absence of the mistake you cannot undo.
roles.empty: The incident is discovered by the customer, and the second customer reads about it.
roles.grades: senior specialist, plus counsel. Improvisation does not work here.

evidence.text: A medical-domain product built under PII constraints: what the model may see, what is stored, what the bot must never say.
An audit background means I read obligations in the source text rather than reconstructing them from a blog post.

roles.limit: I work within the constraints and I know where a specialist is needed. Signing off on regulatory compliance is not my role, and nobody should hand it to me.

complement.seat: Data protection officer / compliance counsel, plus a security engineer if there is a certification target
complement.why: My seat makes theirs possible: clean data boundaries and an honest inventory of what is stored where. It does not replace their work.
complement.when: Before the second customer in a regulated domain. Before the first, if that first one is a hospital.

roles.owns: Scope, sequence and the promises the team makes to people outside it.
roles.measured: Whether the promised date and the promised scope both matched what actually shipped.
roles.empty: Everything is in progress and nothing ships. Status turns into a feeling, and the problems become visible only when optimism stops helping.
roles.grades: mid → lead. Part-time in a small crew, which is why it sits in support rather than core.

evidence.text: Sixteen years of working with data, including forensic engagements delivered into domains that were not mine, on dates that were contractual — scoping, sequencing and defending the result were part of the job.
Lead expert on a data curriculum with a cohort schedule that does not move for anybody.
Empty repository to a production client in five months, with the sequencing decisions that made that possible.

roles.limit: This works up to roughly a dozen people. I own scope, sequencing and delivery. Performance reviews and long-term career work belong to an engineering manager.

complement.why: Past about fifteen people, planning starts taking too much time away from building. One person can no longer do both jobs well.
complement.when: At the third engineer, or the first one who needs a career conversation rather than a task.

roles.owns: Whether the next person can use and maintain what was built without its author.
roles.measured: How many questions arrive that the documentation already answers.
roles.empty: If everything rests on one author, losing that person stops the work. Handing such a system over can take a month.
roles.grades: any grade, but it has to be someone who has built things — technical writing by a non-builder documents the interface and misses the trap.

evidence.text: Four years teaching the data track at Yandex Practicum — the difference between knowing something and being able to hand it over.
A Lua module documented well enough for other volunteers to extend it without my help.

roles.limit: I write internal documentation, decision records and runbooks, and I hand the system over to whoever will maintain it. The copy a customer reads is separate design work.

complement.why: Everything a user reads inside the product — error text, empty states, the bot's own voice — is design work, not writing work.
complement.when: As soon as the product has words in it that a customer reads. In a conversational product, that is day one.

roles.measured: Whether a new user can complete the task without being told how.
roles.empty: A good system loses to a worse one that is easier to use. If the interface is unclear, every demo needs someone explaining it.

evidence.text: I build working interfaces — this page is one of them, written by hand without a framework. Beyond that the designer's work starts: interaction design, a design system and visual identity.

roles.limit: This seat is deliberately open: good design is a separate profession, and pretending an engineer replaces a designer usually means getting an engineer's interface.

complement.seat: A seat for a separate specialist
complement.why: It is the first hire I would make after myself in any crew whose product has a screen. Not the tenth — the first.
complement.when: Before the first customer demo you cannot personally narrate.

roles.owns: The sales pipeline — the conversations that end in signed contracts.
roles.measured: Signed design partners first, repeat sales second.
roles.empty: A well-built product ends up with one user, and the team explains it with marketing problems.
roles.grades: founder-level early, then a real commercial hire. Never an intern.

evidence.text: I can build the model, prepare the numbers for the deck, run the technical part of a customer conversation and talk to their engineers as an equal. But I do not find clients and I do not close deals.

roles.limit: I run the technical part of discovery, demo architecture and the unit-economics side of a commercial conversation. I am a technical partner to a founder, not an outbound sales rep. Finding clients and closing deals is a separate seat.

complement.why: If a technical crew has nobody in this seat, engineering will not fix it. A good product may simply never find customers.
complement.when: Before the engineering starts. This is also the seat I check for in a company before agreeing to join.
